<description>
**Problem:** Setting up an encrypted connection derives six values with the same secret. Each HKDF expansion repeats two SHA256 compressions to hash the same HMAC key pads.

**Fix:** Hash the key pads once per HKDF context, then copy the prepared HMAC state for each expansion. The copy replaces two setup compressions, saving ten SHA256 compressions across the six outputs - the derived bytes stay identical. [RFC 2104 section 4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104.html#section-4) describes this optimization:

[quoted text omitted]

[2026-11-12] c:6833425469 comment by Pranav-error:
Code review ACK (read the diff, didn't build).

The optimization is standard and correct: HKDF-Expand here uses the same PRK for all six expansions, so pre-absorbing the key pads once (`PrepareHMAC` → `m_hmac`) and copying that prepared state per `Expand32` is bit-identical to reconstructing `CHMAC_SHA256(prk, ...)` each time (RFC 2104 §4).

Two things I checked while reviewing:

- `Expand32` is `const` and does `CHMAC_SHA256{m_hmac}` (a copy), so it can't mutate the shared context for later labels — and the new test asserts exactly that ("Expansions must not modify the shared context state"), with the six BIP324 label vectors pinning the outputs.
- The prepared `m_hmac` embeds key-deriving material (as the old `m_prk` did); `BIP324Cipher::Initialize` still does `memory_cleanse(&hkdf, sizeof(hkdf))`, which zeroes the `m_hmac` SHA256 midstates in place, so the "wipe anything that could re-derive the keys" invariant is preserved.

The ~20% on connection setup is a nice win for a hot path. LGTM modulo a Tested ACK from someone who can run `crypto_tests`.
</new_statements>
